title: A* Search and Heuristics

sections.heading: Problem Statement and Informed Search
sections.body:
**Problem.** Input: a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ with a nonnegative edge-weight function $w:E\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$, a source $s\in V$, and a goal $t\in V$ (or, in an implicitly defined state-space graph such as a puzzle, a goal test and a successor function that generates $V$ on demand). Output: a minimum-weight path from $s$ to $t$, i.e. a path $p$ with $w(p)=\delta(s,t)$, or a report that no path exists. Model of computation: the usual comparison-addition model used for Dijkstra and Bellman–Ford, augmented with an oracle heuristic $h:V\to\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}$ that estimates the remaining distance to the goal, with $h(t)=0$ by convention.

A* is a **single-target** shortest-path algorithm: unlike Dijkstra, which computes $\delta(s,v)$ for every $v\in V$ without knowing which vertex is the goal, A* is told $t$ in advance and uses $h$ to steer the search toward it, visiting vertices in order of increasing

$$f(v) = g(v) + h(v),$$

where $g(v)$ is the best path weight discovered so far from $s$ to $v$ — exactly Dijkstra's tentative distance $d[v]$ — and $h(v)$ is the heuristic's estimate of $\delta(v,t)$. Setting $h \equiv 0$ makes $f=g$ everywhere, and A* becomes literally Dijkstra's algorithm; everything below is really about what a good choice of $h$ buys over that baseline.

sections.heading: Admissible and Consistent Heuristics
sections.body:
**Admissible.** $h$ is admissible if $h(v) \le \delta(v,t)$ for every $v \in V$: it never overestimates the true remaining cost. **Consistent** (or monotone) is the stronger, edge-local condition

$$h(u) \le w(u,v) + h(v) \ \text{ for every edge } (u,v)\in E,$$

together with $h(t)=0$.

Consistency implies admissibility: telescope the inequality along any shortest path $v=v_0, v_1,\dots,v_k=t$ to get $h(v) \le \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} w(v_i,v_{i+1}) = \delta(v,t)$. The converse fails — one can patch an admissible $h$ to dip sharply at a single vertex while staying below every $\delta(v,t)$, which satisfies admissibility but violates the edge-local bound at that vertex.

In practice almost every heuristic used in a real search is consistent, because it is obtained by solving a *relaxed* version of the same shortest-path problem — straight-line distance for Euclidean road networks, Manhattan distance for a grid with unit moves, the count of misplaced tiles or a pattern-database lower bound for sliding-tile puzzles — and a relaxed-problem distance automatically satisfies the triangle inequality that consistency demands, since dropping constraints can only shorten paths. The distinction matters operationally: the textbook *graph-search* version of A*, which closes a vertex permanently the first time it is popped and never reopens it, is only guaranteed optimal when $h$ is consistent; with a merely admissible $h$ it may need to reopen closed vertices to stay correct, which the proof below makes precise.

sections.heading: Mechanism: A* as Dijkstra with Reduced Costs
sections.body:
**Reduction.** Define the reduced cost of edge $(u,v)$ as

$$\hat w(u,v) = w(u,v) + h(v) - h(u).$$

If $h$ is consistent, $\hat w(u,v) \ge 0$ for every edge — this is exactly the consistency inequality rearranged. This is the same reweighting trick Johnson's algorithm uses to strip negative weights before running Dijkstra, except the potential function here is the heuristic itself rather than a Bellman–Ford distance.

Telescoping $\hat w$ along any $s$–$v$ path $p$ gives

$$\hat w(p) = w(p) + h(v) - h(s).$$

Every path from $s$ to a fixed vertex $v$ has its true weight shifted by the same additive constant $h(v)-h(s)$, so the *ordering* of path weights — and in particular which path is shortest — is unchanged by the reduction. Running Dijkstra on $(G,\hat w)$ from $s$ therefore computes the same shortest-path tree as running it on $(G,w)$. Dijkstra's tentative distance on the reduced graph after reaching $v$ is $\hat d(v) = g(v) + h(v) - h(s) = f(v) - h(s)$: a constant shift of A*'s own priority key. Since Dijkstra always extracts the vertex of minimum $\hat d$ and A* always extracts the vertex of minimum $f = \hat d + h(s)$, the two algorithms extract vertices in exactly the same order. A* is Dijkstra's algorithm on the reduced-cost graph $(G,\hat w)$, nonnegative by consistency, with the priority key relabeled — nothing about which vertex gets finalized when actually changes.

sections.heading: Correctness of A* with a Consistent Heuristic
sections.body:
**Theorem.** If $h$ is consistent, then whenever A* pops (closes) a vertex $u$, $g(u) = \delta(s,u)$.

*Proof*, by contradiction on pop order — the same strategy used for Dijkstra's own correctness theorem. Suppose $u$ is the first vertex popped with $g(u) > \delta(s,u)$; since $g(s)=0=\delta(s,s)$, $u \ne s$. Let $y$ be the first vertex along a shortest $s$–$u$ path that is not yet closed, with predecessor $x$ on that same path. Because $u$ is the first violator, every vertex closed before $u$ — in particular $x$, if $x \ne s$ — already has $g(x)=\delta(s,x)$. Expanding $x$ relaxed edge $(x,y)$, so $g(y) \le g(x) + w(x,y) = \delta(s,x)+w(x,y) = \delta(s,y)$ (the last equality because $x$ lies on a shortest path to $y$); combined with the trivial $g(y)\ge \delta(s,y)$, this forces $g(y)=\delta(s,y)$ exactly.

Now compare $f$-values. Since $y$ lies on a shortest $s$–$u$ path, $\delta(s,y)+\delta(y,u)=\delta(s,u)$, and consistency telescoped along a shortest $y$–$u$ path gives $h(y) \le \delta(y,u)+h(u)$. Adding $\delta(s,y)$ to both sides and substituting $g(y)=\delta(s,y)$:

$$f(y) = \delta(s,y) + h(y) \le \delta(s,u) + h(u).$$

Because $g(u) > \delta(s,u)$ by assumption, the right side is strictly less than $g(u)+h(u)=f(u)$, so $f(y) < f(u)$. But $y$ was already in the open set (inserted when $x$ was closed) and not yet closed, so A* should have popped $y$ no later than $u$ — contradicting that $u$ was the vertex of minimum $f$ extracted at that step. No such first violator can exist, so $g(u)=\delta(s,u)$ at every pop: exactly Dijkstra's own correctness argument, with $f$ in place of $d$ as the priority key.

sections.heading: Running Time, Variants, and IDA*
sections.body:
**Running time.** A*'s control structure is identical to Dijkstra's — only the priority key changes from $g$ to $f=g+h$ — so the same cost table applies (below), counting $V'$ and $E'$ as the vertices and edges actually generated before the goal is popped. With a binary heap the bound is $O((V'+E')\lg V')$; with a Fibonacci heap it is $O(E' + V'\lg V')$ amortized, mirroring the array/binary-heap/Fibonacci-heap comparison used for plain Dijkstra. A*'s practical payoff is not a better worst-case bound — on an uninformative heuristic it degenerates to Dijkstra's full $\Theta(V)$-vertex, $\Theta(E)$-edge cost exactly — but a much smaller $V',E'$ in practice, because any vertex with $f(v) > \delta(s,t)$ can never lie on an optimal path and is never popped.

**IDA\*.** Iterative-deepening A* replaces the priority queue (and its $\Theta(V)$ memory) with repeated depth-first searches bounded by an increasing $f$-cost threshold: each pass prunes any branch with $f=g+h$ above the current threshold and raises the threshold to the smallest $f$-value seen just beyond it. Memory is $O(d)$ for solution depth/cost $d$, not $O(V)$, which is why IDA* — not A* — is the standard choice for huge implicit state spaces such as the 15-puzzle or Rubik's cube, where the visited-state count would never fit in memory. If each successive threshold increases the frontier geometrically (branching factor $b>1$), the total work across all iterations is within a constant factor of $b/(b-1)$ of the final, most expensive iteration alone, so the asymptotic time is the same order as a single bounded depth-first search at cost $d$.

no heap needed; competitive when the graph is dense

code.caption: A* with a consistent heuristic; priority key f = g + h degenerates to Dijkstra when h ≡ 0. This exact script produced the worked example below.

worked_example.problem: Run A* with a consistent heuristic on the weighted undirected graph with vertices $\{S,A,B,C,G\}$ and edges $S\!-\!A{:}1,\ S\!-\!B{:}4,\ A\!-\!B{:}2,\ A\!-\!C{:}5,\ B\!-\!C{:}1,\ B\!-\!G{:}5,\ C\!-\!G{:}2$, start $S$, goal $G$, and heuristic $h(S){=}5, h(A){=}4, h(B){=}2, h(C){=}1, h(G){=}0$. Verify $h$ is consistent, trace every pop and every $g$-value update, and confirm the result against an independent shortest-path computation.
worked_example.solution:
**Consistency check.** True distances to $G$ are $\delta(C,G)=2$, $\delta(B,G)=3$ (via $B\!-\!C\!-\!G$), $\delta(A,G)=5$ (via $A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!G$), $\delta(S,G)=6$ (via $S\!-\!A\!-\!B\!-\!C\!-\!G$). Every $h(v) \le \delta(v,G)$ (admissible), and $h(u) \le w(u,v)+h(v)$ holds with equality on every edge of the optimal path and with slack elsewhere (consistent) — e.g. $h(S)=5 \le w(S,A)+h(A)=1+4=5$.

**Trace** ($f=g+h$ shown at each pop):

| Popped | g | f | Updates performed on expansion |
|---|---|---|---|
| S | 0 | 5 | insert A: g=1, f=5; insert B: g=4, f=6 |
| A | 1 | 5 | improve B: g=1+2=3, f=5; insert C: g=1+5=6, f=7 |
| B | 3 | 5 | improve C: g=3+1=4, f=5; insert G: g=3+5=8, f=8 |
| C | 4 | 5 | improve G: g=4+2=6, f=6 |
| G | 6 | 6 | goal popped — stop |

The returned path, read off the parent pointers set at each improving update, is $S \to A \to B \to C \to G$ with weight $1+2+1+2=6$, matching $\delta(S,G)=6$ computed independently above. Note that B and C are each updated once *while still open* and are never touched again after being closed — exactly the behavior consistency guarantees, so no vertex is ever reopened.

**Cross-check via the reduction.** The reduced weights $\hat w(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)-h(u)$ are $\hat w(S,A){=}0, \hat w(S,B){=}1, \hat w(A,B){=}0, \hat w(A,C){=}2, \hat w(B,C){=}0, \hat w(B,G){=}3, \hat w(C,G){=}1$ — all $\ge 0$, as consistency guarantees. Running ordinary Dijkstra on these reduced weights from $S$ pops vertices in the identical order $S,A,B,C,G$ and reaches $G$ with reduced distance $\hat d(G)=1$; recovering the true cost via $w(p)=\hat d(G)-h(G)+h(S)=1-0+5=6$ reproduces the same answer, confirming that A* on this instance really is Dijkstra on $(G,\hat w)$.

pitfalls: Admissible but inconsistent heuristics break the standard graph-search implementation: the closed-list version that never reopens a popped vertex is only proven optimal under consistency (see the correctness proof); with a merely admissible h, a later-discovered cheaper path to an already-closed vertex can be missed unless closed vertices are reopened on improvement.

Forgetting h(t)=0: if the heuristic does not vanish at the goal, the reduction ŵ(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)-h(u) no longer telescopes to the true path weight, and the algorithm can report a goal cost off by a constant, or terminate at the wrong vertex when several goals are acceptable.

Negative edge weights are not rescued by a 'consistent' heuristic. A* inherits Dijkstra's requirement that w ≥ 0 (equivalently ŵ ≥ 0 after reduction); Dijkstra's single-pop-per-vertex correctness argument itself assumes nonnegative weights, so negative edges need a Bellman-Ford-based method instead.

Admissibility against the wrong target: with several acceptable goal vertices, h(v) must underestimate the distance to the nearest one, not to one fixed goal; a heuristic tuned for a single target can overestimate once there are multiple goals and lose optimality.

Floating-point heuristics that round the wrong way: a geometric heuristic such as Euclidean distance computed in floating point can round up by an epsilon and silently violate admissibility; such estimates should be rounded down (floored), never to the nearest value.
applications: Game and robotics pathfinding: grid or navigation-mesh movement runs A* with an octile or Euclidean heuristic, because the state graph is explicit, small enough for an open/closed list, and the heuristic is cheap and consistent by the triangle inequality.

Road-network routing with landmarks (the ALT algorithm, Goldberg and Harrelson): distances to a handful of precomputed landmark vertices give a provably consistent heuristic via the triangle inequality, yielding a large practical speedup over plain Dijkstra on continental-scale road networks.

Puzzle and combinatorial search with IDA*: sliding-tile puzzles (8-puzzle, 15-puzzle) and Rubik's-cube solvers use IDA* with Manhattan-distance or pattern-database heuristics because the reachable state space is far too large for an explicit open/closed list, while recursion depth stays bounded by the solution length.

Automated planning: STRIPS-style planners search the plan-state graph with A* or weighted A*, using a relaxed-planning-graph heuristic obtained by dropping delete effects — itself a consistent heuristic because relaxation can only shorten the true plan length.

self_check.question: Why is the graph-search (closed-list, never-reopen) implementation of A* only guaranteed to find a shortest path when the heuristic is consistent, rather than merely admissible?
self_check.answer: The correctness proof shows that when A* pops a vertex u it has g(u)=\delta(s,u), and the key step is bounding f(y) < f(u) for the first not-yet-closed vertex y on a shortest path to u. That bound uses the edge-local triangle inequality h(y) \le \delta(y,u) + h(u), telescoped along the shortest y-u path — this is consistency, not mere admissibility. Admissibility only bounds h at individual vertices against \delta(v,t); it says nothing about how h changes from one vertex to a neighbor, so f-values need not be monotone non-decreasing along a path. With a merely admissible h, a vertex can be closed with a g-value that a cheaper path discovered later would have improved, and the closed-list version has no mechanism to revisit it. Tree-search A* (which never permanently closes anything) stays correct with only admissibility; the graph-search version needs consistency, or must reopen closed vertices when a strictly smaller g is found.

self_check.question: In the worked example, B enters the open set with g=4, f=6 after S is expanded, then is updated to g=3, f=5 after A is expanded. By how much does f(B) drop, and why does this update never require reopening a closed vertex?
self_check.answer: f(B) drops from 6 to 5, a decrease of 1 (equivalently g(B) drops from 4 to 3, since h(B)=2 is unchanged). This is an ordinary decrease-key on a vertex that is still in the open set: B had not been popped yet when A was expanded, so updating its g-value is exactly what a priority queue's decrease-key operation is for. The correctness theorem guarantees that once a vertex is popped (closed) under a consistent heuristic, its g-value already equals the true distance \delta(s,v), so no closed vertex is ever revisited; every update A* performs targets a vertex that is either new or still open, never one already finalized.

self_check.question: Let h1 and h2 be two admissible heuristics for the same shortest-path problem, and define h(n) = max(h1(n), h2(n)). Prove h is admissible and dominates both, and show that if h1 and h2 are also consistent, h is consistent too.
self_check.answer: Admissibility: for every vertex n, h1(n) \le h^*(n) and h2(n) \le h^*(n), where h^*(n)=\delta(n,t) is the true remaining cost; taking the max of two quantities each bounded above by h^*(n) keeps the max bounded by h^*(n) as well, so h(n) \le h^*(n) and h is admissible. Dominance: by definition h(n) \ge h1(n) and h(n) \ge h2(n) for every n, so h is at least as informed as either component, which can only reduce the number of vertices A* needs to expand. Consistency: suppose h1, h2 are both consistent and fix an edge (u,v). Say h(u) = h_i(u) for whichever index i achieves the maximum at u. Then h(u) = h_i(u) \le w(u,v) + h_i(v) (consistency of h_i) \le w(u,v) + h(v) (since h(v) \ge h_i(v) by definition of the max). This is exactly the consistency inequality for h, so the pointwise maximum of finitely many consistent heuristics is again consistent. This is why practical A* implementations combine several cheap heuristics (e.g. several pattern databases) by taking their pointwise maximum rather than committing to a single one.

key_points: A* expands vertices by increasing f(v)=g(v)+h(v); h≡0 makes A* literally Dijkstra's algorithm.
Consistent: h(u) ≤ w(u,v)+h(v) on every edge, h(t)=0; consistency ⇒ admissibility (h(v)≤δ(v,t)), not conversely.
A* = Dijkstra on the reduced graph ŵ(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)-h(u) ≥ 0, same vertex-pop order as plain Dijkstra.
Correctness (consistent h): when A* pops u, g(u)=δ(s,u) — same proof strategy as Dijkstra's own theorem.
IDA* trades A*'s O(V) open/closed list for O(d) memory via repeated depth-first searches bounded by an f-cost threshold.
The max of admissible (or consistent) heuristics is again admissible (or consistent) and dominates both.
tagline: A* expands nodes by f=g+h; with a consistent heuristic it is exactly Dijkstra on reduced costs — same optimality, far fewer vertices expanded.
tldr: A* Search extends Dijkstra's algorithm with a heuristic $h$, expanding vertices in order of $f(v)=g(v)+h(v)$ instead of $g(v)$ alone. When $h$ is **consistent** ($h(u)\le w(u,v)+h(v)$ on every edge), A* is exactly Dijkstra's algorithm run on the reduced-cost graph $\hat w(u,v)=w(u,v)+h(v)-h(u)\ge 0$, so it inherits Dijkstra's optimality guarantee while typically expanding far fewer vertices than plain Dijkstra. **IDA\*** keeps the same guarantee but trades the $O(V)$ priority queue for $O(d)$ memory via repeated depth-bounded searches, which is why it — not A* — is the standard choice for implicit state spaces too large to hold in an open/closed list.
